t: Maximum Empty Axis-Aligned Rectangle — Corner Enumeration
o: Choose four points as corners of an axis-aligned rectangle containing no other point inside or on its border; maximize area. With at most 10 points, exhaustive search is trivial. Example 3 shows a larger rectangle can be invalidated by a boundary point ([1,1],[3,1],[3,3],[1,3] fails once [1,2],[3,2] appear), while the height-2 rectangles remain valid. Checking 'empty' means no fifth point lies in the closed bounding box other than the four corners themselves.
k: A valid corner set is exactly: two distinct x-coordinates and two distinct y-coordinates, with all four (x,y) combinations present.
Emptiness check = no other point with x1 <= x <= x2 and y1 <= y <= y2, excluding the four corners.

a.i: Try every 4-combination of points; accept it as a rectangle when the sorted x's pair up and the sorted y's pair up; then scan all points for intruders. C(10,4)=210 combinations times a 10-point scan — instantaneous.
s: For each 4-combination, sort the x's and y's.
Scan every input point inside the closed box, skipping the four corners; if none, update the answer with (x2-x1)*(y2-y1).
a.t: O(C(n,4) * n) — about 210 * 10 operations at n = 10.
a.sp: O(n) — the point set for corner lookups.

a.i: Every axis-aligned rectangle is identified by one diagonal: opposite corners (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) with x1<x2, y1<y2. Require the two reflected corners to exist as points, then run the same emptiness scan. This halves the enumeration to O(n^2) candidate diagonals and reads more naturally.
s: For each ordered pair with x1<x2 and y1<y2, check (x1,y2) and (x2,y1) exist.
Scan all points inside the closed box excluding the four corners.
a.t: O(n^3) — O(n^2) diagonals each with an O(n) emptiness scan.

w: With n <= 10 anything works; present the diagonal version as the cleaner formulation. Pitfalls: the emptiness test must exclude the four corners themselves (they are inside the closed box by definition), and 'on its border' counts as invalid, hence the closed-interval check. Follow-up: the harder versions (3381+) raise n to 1e5, demanding sweep-line + BIT techniques to find, for each diagonal, whether any point lies inside.
